title: Wi-Fi Penetration Testing
learning_objectives: Set up a wireless adapter in monitoring mode for Wi-Fi testing
Capture WPA2 handshakes and crack them offline
Execute deauthentication attacks to force handshake capture
Understand evil twin and rogue AP attack scenarios
Recognize WPA3 improvements and remaining wireless attack vectors

post_assessment.question: What must you capture before cracking a WPA2 password offline?
options: The 4-way EAPOL handshake between a client and the access point
A full data stream from one client
post_assessment.explanation: WPA2 cracking requires capturing the 4-way EAPOL handshake. This handshake contains the material needed to test password candidates offline.

post_assessment.question: What is the purpose of a deauthentication attack in Wi-Fi pentesting?
options: To force clients to reconnect, generating a new handshake that the attacker can capture
To gain admin access to the router
post_assessment.explanation: Deauth attacks send fake disassociation frames to force devices off the network. When they reconnect, a new handshake is generated — which the attacker captures.

post_assessment.question: An evil twin attack works by:
options: Creating a rogue AP with the same SSID as the target, tricking clients into connecting
post_assessment.explanation: An evil twin AP mimics the legitimate network's SSID (and sometimes MAC). Clients may auto-connect to the stronger signal, routing all their traffic through the attacker.

post_assessment.question: Which aircrack-ng tool puts a wireless adapter into monitoring mode?
post_assessment.explanation: airmon-ng enables monitor mode on a wireless interface, allowing you to passively capture all wireless traffic on a channel.

post_assessment.question: What security improvement does WPA3-SAE provide over WPA2-PSK?
options: Protection against offline dictionary attacks on captured handshakes
post_assessment.explanation: WPA3 uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) which prevents offline dictionary attacks. Even if an attacker captures the exchange, they cannot brute-force the password offline like with WPA2.

jim_kwik_principles.forget: Forget that Wi-Fi is 'just a network connection' — it's an over-the-air attack surface accessible from the parking lot
jim_kwik_principles.active: Set up a test AP and adapter, capture a handshake, and crack it with aircrack-ng before finishing this lesson
jim_kwik_principles.state: Approach each wireless engagement as if any employee's traffic could be intercepted from outside
jim_kwik_principles.teach: Explain deauth attacks as 'forcibly kicking someone off Wi-Fi so you can watch them log back in'
jim_kwik_principles.enter: Before wireless testing, verify you have explicit written authorization — wireless pentesting is legally sensitive
jim_kwik_principles.review: After each capture, verify: did I get the full 4-way handshake? Partial captures waste cracking time
jim_kwik_principles.notes: Document: BSSID, channel, encryption, clients, handshake captured (Y/N), crack result
jim_kwik_principles.why: Wi-Fi pentesting is part of every physical red team engagement and many compliance assessments
jim_kwik_principles.emotion: The thrill of cracking a WPA2 password from a captured handshake in under a minute
jim_kwik_principles.speed: Use hashcat with GPU acceleration instead of aircrack-ng CPU for dramatically faster WPA2 cracking

content_blocks.title: Over-the-Air Means Over-the-Fence
content_blocks.content: Wi-Fi signals don't respect walls or property lines. An attacker in a parking lot, a coffee shop next door, or a car on the street can intercept wireless traffic. This physical accessibility makes wireless security uniquely important — and wireless pentesting a critical skill for red teams. Every organization with Wi-Fi has an attack surface that extends beyond their physical perimeter.

content_blocks.title: Wi-Fi Security Protocols
content_blocks.content: Understanding what you're attacking is the first step.

subsections.title: WPA2-PSK (Most Common)
subsections.content: Pre-Shared Key mode. All users share the same password. The 4-way EAPOL handshake ensures both sides know the password without transmitting it directly. Vulnerability: captured handshake can be cracked offline with dictionary/brute force attacks.

subsections.title: WPA2-Enterprise
subsections.content: Uses RADIUS server and individual credentials (EAP). No shared password. Harder to attack but vulnerable to evil twin + fake RADIUS (credential harvesting).

subsections.title: WPA3-SAE
subsections.content: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals. Prevents offline dictionary attacks — even with a captured exchange, password can't be cracked offline. Also provides forward secrecy: past traffic can't be decrypted even if the password is later compromised.

content_blocks.title: Teach Me Like I'm 10: Wi-Fi Hacking
content_blocks.content: Imagine everyone at school passes notes to the teacher through the air instead of handing them directly.

subsections.title: The attacks
subsections.content:
Handshake capture: you wait until someone new walks in and says the secret password to the teacher. You write down exactly what they said.

Deauth attack: you push someone out of the classroom so they have to walk back in and say the password again — you're listening this time.

Evil twin: you sit outside the classroom door wearing a teacher costume. Students think you're the real teacher and give you their passwords.

Cracking: you take home the 'secret handshake' you wrote down and try every word in the dictionary until you find one that matches.

content_blocks.title: WPA2 Handshake Capture and Crack
content_blocks.description: Full aircrack-ng workflow from monitoring to cracking
content_blocks.code:
# Step 1: Enable monitor mode
sudo airmon-ng start wlan0
# Interface becomes wlan0mon

# Step 2: Scan for networks
sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon
# Note: BSSID, channel, and ESSID of target

# Step 3: Target specific AP and capture
sudo airodump-ng -c 6 --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -w capture wlan0mon
# Wait for 4-way handshake... or force it:

# Step 4: Deauth a client to force reconnection (separate terminal)
sudo aireplay-ng -0 5 -a AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -c 11:22:33:44:55:66 wlan0mon
# -0 5 = send 5 deauth frames
# -a = target AP BSSID
# -c = target client MAC

# Step 5: Verify handshake captured
# airodump-ng will show "WPA handshake: AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF"

# Step 6: Crack with dictionary
sudo aircrack-ng -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt capture-01.cap

# Alternative: Crack with hashcat (GPU - much faster)
hccapx_file=$(aircrack-ng capture-01.cap -J hashcat_file)
hashcat -m 22000 hashcat_file.hc22000 rockyou.txt
content_blocks.instructions:
1. Ensure you have a compatible wireless adapter (Alfa AWUS036ACH recommended)
2. Enable monitor mode with airmon-ng
3. Scan and identify your test network
4. Start targeted capture on the correct channel
5. Use deauth to force a handshake if no clients are connecting
6. Verify the handshake is captured before stopping
7. Crack with aircrack-ng (CPU) or hashcat (GPU)
content_blocks.expected_outcome: A captured .cap file containing the 4-way handshake, and a cracked password (if it's in your wordlist). Common weak passwords crack in seconds, strong passwords may resist dictionary attacks entirely.

content_blocks.title: PMKID Attack: No Handshake Needed (2018)
content_blocks.scenario: Security researcher Jens Steube (hashcat developer) discovered that WPA2 routers broadcast a PMKID value in the first message of the 4-way handshake. Unlike the traditional handshake attack, the PMKID can be captured without any connected clients — no deauth needed, no waiting. The PMKID is derived from the PSK and can be cracked offline, just like the full handshake. This reduced WPA2 attacks from 'wait for a handshake' to 'scan and go'.
key_lessons: New attack techniques can make previously difficult attacks trivial
No connected clients required for PMKID — just scan the AP's beacon
Tools like hcxdumptool automate PMKID capture
WPA3-SAE is immune to PMKID attacks — another reason to migrate

content_blocks.title: Wi-Fi Pentesting Workflow: MSCDC
content_blocks.explanation: M=Monitor mode (airmon-ng start wlan0), S=Scan networks (airodump-ng), C=Capture target (airodump-ng with BSSID/channel filter), D=Deauth clients (aireplay-ng -0), C=Crack handshake (aircrack-ng or hashcat). Follow this order, every time.

content_blocks.title: Wireless Security in Your Environment
prompts: Is your organization still using WPA2-PSK? When was the password last changed?
What would happen if an attacker cracked your corporate Wi-Fi password from the parking lot?
Could a rogue AP be set up near your office without anyone noticing?
How would you detect a deauthentication attack against your wireless network?

content_blocks.title: Physical Meets Digital
content_blocks.content: Wi-Fi pentesting sits at the intersection of physical and digital security. It's one of the most immediately impactful skills on a red team engagement. A cracked WPA2 password means internal network access — often bypassing firewalls, NAC, and VPN requirements entirely. The tools are free, the hardware is cheap, and the technique is reliable. Master this skill.
